title: Wait for one another (1 Corinthians 11:17–34)
hookLine: at their suppers some eat first and some go hungry; Paul hands on the words of the Lord's Supper
tomorrow: can a foot quit the body? Paul lets one try.

cards: Every potluck has an early crowd. They fill their plates with the good stuff, and whoever comes off the late shift finds a spoon in an empty dish and a paper plate.

Corinth had it worse, and at church, at the Lord's Supper, a meal that was meant to be holy and shared. "For in eating every one taketh before other his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken."
Paul has been praising them. Now he stops: "I praise you not."

teach.b: Paul is sharp: "What? have ye not houses to eat and to drink in? or despise ye the church of God, and shame them that have not?"

teach.h: THIS DO IN REMEMBRANCE OF ME.
teach.b: Then he hands on what he says he received: "the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread," gave thanks, broke it, and said, "Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me."
Then the cup. Then a warning about eating "unworthily," "not discerning the Lord's body." Which body?
Here Christians read it two ways, and both have a real case.
Some, among them Catholic and Orthodox Christians, hear the bread. Christ is truly present in it, so eating carelessly misses him.

Their best case: Paul has just quoted, this is my body; the word points straight back to the bread. Others, among them some Protestant readers, hear the people. The church is the body, and a chapter later Paul says so.
Their best case: the failure Paul names here isn't bad manners at the altar. It's shaming the hungry. Some hold both at once.
Paul's fix serves either reading: "Wherefore, my brethren, when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another."
And if you're starving? "let him eat at home."

how: Christians share the Lord's Supper, also called communion or the Eucharist, using Paul's words from this chapter; churches differ on how often and on how Christ is present in the bread and cup.

games.q: what does “wait for one another” mean?
o: taking turns to speak at a meeting
fasting together until a meal starts
sharing a meal so no one is left out

games.q: wait for one another — tap the pairs.
p: Christ truly present in the bread

s: Paul's complaint at Corinth was about who ate first and who went hungry
one is hungry, and another is drunken... shame them that have not.
there's only one way Christians read 'not discerning the Lord's body'
some hear the bread, some the gathered church, and some both at once.
Paul says he received the words of the Lord's Supper and handed them on
for I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you.

games.q: a friend at youth group reads 'not discerning the Lord's body' as the bread itself. you lean toward 'the people.' what's her best case?
o: Paul has just quoted 'this is my body'; the word points back to the bread.
Paul never mentions bread anywhere in this part of the letter.
Paul cared about the bread, so the hungry people didn't matter to him.
games.why: the bread reading leans on the words right before the warning: take, eat: this is my body. the people reading leans on the shamed hungry. some readers hold both.

practice: Pour a glass of water, or picture one in front of you. Before you drink, wait. Hold the glass, and let the people who'd share your table this week come to mind: the late one, the quiet one, the one who eats less.
Then take one slow sip, as if every one of them already had a plate.

wordCard.voice: Wait for one another. Paul's plain fix for a holy meal that had split the full from the hungry.

orig.note: Greek: remembrance. the word behind this do in remembrance of me.

carryVoice: Your line: discern the body. Some hear the bread, some the people, and Paul's fix serves both. That's today.
